I've written the report. The main finding is that ash dieback would cost more carbon than replanting can win back within 30 years.

- **Trees outside the forest:** in the 25 km² Breckland sample area the model covers, hedgerow and field trees hold about 925 t of carbon (about 590–1,260 t). That is under 1 t per hectare, because trees cover only about 1% of the land. Hedges under 3 m tall aren't counted, so hedgerow carbon is underestimated.
- **Ash dieback:** by 2055 the trees would hold about 84 t less carbon than without dieback, roughly 8% less. They would also absorb about 700 t less CO2 over 30 years. This assumes 15% of broadleaved trees are ash and 80% of those die. Those are the model's defaults, because no map gives the local ash share.
- **Replanting:** replacing every dead ash tree puts back only about 8 t of carbon by 2055, about a tenth of the loss. Replanting half of them puts back about 4 t. Young trees grow slowly, so the gain from replanting comes after 2055.
- **Thetford Forest:** average biomass fell from 108.9 to 102.9 tonnes per hectare between 2015 and 2024. The change is not statistically significant, so it shouldn't be described publicly as the forest "losing carbon". About 1,009 ha lost biomass and 493 ha gained, which fits rotational felling. No cause can be assigned without felling or storm records.
- **Grassland and livestock:** within 15 km of central Breckland, the habitat map shows about 21,600 ha of semi-natural grassland and 2,600 ha of dwarf shrub heath. Grazing is light, at 0.21 livestock units per hectare: mostly about 20,300 sheep and 3,300 beef and other cattle, plus about 1,900 dairy cattle. The map doesn't show habitat condition, so this isn't 21,600 ha of good-quality grassland.

The 15 km circle only approximates "the same area" and doesn't match the tree sample area or the forest boundary exactly. None of the models cover species, habitat condition, water or soil carbon.

The report includes two charts, wording that is safe for public use, and suggested next steps. Your own count of ash trees would make the dieback scenario much more reliable.
